generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: The boxy one everyone wants now. Light, simple, and honest, the 325i's straight-six and the first M3 both came from this shell.

generations.name: Fourth generation
generations.note: Arguably the sweet spot: modern safety and refinement, hydraulic steering with real feel, and proportions that still look right.

generations.name: Seventh generation
generations.note: Bigger and more digital, but the M340i's B58 straight-six is one of the best engines BMW has ever made.

models.intro: The sports sedan benchmark for fifty years. Other brands build rivals; BMW builds the car they are measured against. The recipe has swollen and softened at times, but a straight-six 3 Series driven hard is still the reference.

generations.name: Fourth generation
generations.note: The high-water mark. Every control weighted perfectly, and the M5's V8 manual remains a collector-grade high.

generations.name: Sixth generation
generations.note: Softer and more luxurious, chasing the E-Class buyer. Fast and comfortable, less of a driver's car than what came before.

generations.name: Seventh generation
generations.note: A correction back toward balance. The 540i pairs the B58 six with a chassis that finally remembered the badge.

models.intro: The executive sedan done the BMW way: rear-drive balance, a proper straight-six up front, and just enough aggression. At its best, the E39, it was possibly the finest sedan in the world.

models.collectorNote: E30 values are driven by originality and motorsport provenance. A documented, unmodified car is worth far more than a faster modified one.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Box flares, a dog-leg gearbox, and a four-cylinder that revved like it meant it. Still the most successful touring car of its era.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: The S54 straight-six at 8,000 rpm, a proper manual, and steering you can read a newspaper through. The one most people picture.

generations.name: Sixth generation
generations.note: Twin-turbo power, available all-wheel drive, and, finally, in the Touring, a wagon. The grille debate never touched the way it drives.

models.intro: Born as a homologation special for touring-car racing, kept as the fast 3 Series with its own engine, chassis, and attitude. The market treats it as its own model, and so does everyone who has driven one.

models.collectorNote: Rust is the whole negotiation. The tii and Turbo command serious premiums, verify numbers and injection hardware, because clones exist.

generations.name: Production run
generations.note: The tii's fuel injection was exotic in 1971; the 1973 Turbo, with mirror-written script on its spoiler, was Europe's first turbocharged production car.

models.intro: The car that saved BMW in America and invented the sports sedan formula: a boxy two-door, a willing four-cylinder, and handling that made contemporary Detroit iron feel broken. Every 3 Series since is an apology for, or a tribute to, this car.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Range Rover underpinnings in its bones, BMW engines up front. The 4.4i V8 was the one to have.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: Seven seats arrived, and so did the twin-turbo era. The X5 M that followed made over 550 hp, which tells you where this was heading.

generations.name: Fourth generation
generations.note: Air suspension, a plug-in hybrid option, and the B58 six doing quiet, effortless work. The default luxury family hauler for people who still care about engines.

models.intro: BMW insisted on calling it a Sports Activity Vehicle, and for once the marketing was honest: the X5 drove like a tall 5 Series when every rival drove like a truck. It built the performance-SUV segment the whole industry now lives in.

models.collectorNote: The most collectible BMW ever made. Procars with period race history sit at the top of the market; road cars follow, with low-mileage originality prized over restoration.

generations.name: M1 road car
generations.note: 453 cars were built in total, 399 of them road cars. The M88 3.5 litre straight-six, a development of the racing CSL engine, made 277 hp. When the Lamborghini deal collapsed, BMW took production back and Baur finished the cars.

generations.name: M1 Procar
generations.note: Homologation delays left the M1 with nowhere to race, so BMW invented the Procar Championship as a Grand Prix support series: privateers against the five fastest F1 qualifiers in identical 470 hp cars. Niki Lauda won in 1979, Nelson Piquet in 1980.

models.intro: BMW's first mid-engined car and the first product of BMW Motorsport. Giugiaro styled it, Lamborghini was meant to build it and could not, and the M1 ended up famous less for its road career than for Procar, the one-make series that put Grand Prix drivers in identical cars.
